A mosque is a building where Muslims — followers of the religion of Islam — go to worship God (whom they call Allah in Arabic). It is the central place of religious life for Muslims, much like a church is for Christians or a temple is for Hindus.

A mosque is a place of prayer. The word refers to any dedicated space — from a grand, domed building to a modest room — where Muslims gather to pray and connect with their faith. The prayers performed there are directed solely toward God; Muslims do not worship any statue, idol, or image inside a mosque. In fact, you will find no pictures or sculptures of people or animals inside a mosque, as Islamic tradition discourages representing living beings in a place of worship.
What a mosque typically looks like

Most mosques, especially traditional ones, share a set of recognizable features:

  • A dome: The large, rounded roof that covers the main prayer hall. It is both architectural and symbolic — it represents the vault of the heavens and helps the sound of prayer carry inside.
  • A minaret: A tall, slender tower attached to or standing beside the mosque. Historically, a person called a muezzin would climb to the top of the minaret and call out the adhan (the call to prayer) five times a day to alert the surrounding community that it was time to pray. Today, this call is often made through a loudspeaker mounted on the minaret.
  • A mihrab: A small arched niche or alcove carved into one of the interior walls. It marks the direction of Mecca — the holiest city in Islam, located in present-day Saudi Arabia. When Muslims pray, they must face Mecca, and the mihrab tells them exactly which direction that is.
  • A minbar: A raised platform or pulpit, usually made of wood, located next to the mihrab. The imam (the religious leader who leads prayer) stands on it to deliver the sermon, especially during Friday prayers.
  • An open courtyard: Many mosques have a large courtyard outside or surrounding the main prayer hall. This provides additional space for worshippers when the hall is full.
  • A place for ritual washing (wudu): Before Muslims enter the prayer hall to pray, they must perform wudu — a ritual purification that involves washing the hands, face, arms, and feet with water. Mosques always have a designated area (with taps or fountains) for this purpose.
  • Carpeted floors: The prayer hall is almost always carpeted. Worshippers remove their shoes before entering and pray directly on the carpet, which keeps the space clean and dignified.
  • No furniture in the prayer hall: Unlike a church with pews or a cinema with seats, the main prayer hall of a mosque is typically open and bare — just carpeted floor. This is because Islamic prayer involves standing, bowing, and prostrating (touching the forehead to the ground), and worshippers need open floor space to do this.

A mosque serves several important functions:

1. The five daily prayers
Muslims are required to pray five times a day: before sunrise (Fajr), at midday (Dhuhr), in the afternoon (Asr), just after sunset (Maghrib), and at night (Isha). While Muslims can pray anywhere that is clean — at home, at work, outdoors — praying together in a mosque is considered especially virtuous. Worshippers stand in straight rows, shoulder to shoulder, and pray in unison behind the imam.

2. The Friday prayer (Jumu'ah)
Friday holds special significance in Islam. The midday prayer on Friday — called Jumu'ah — is a congregational prayer that Muslims are strongly encouraged (and in many traditions, obligated) to attend at the mosque. It includes a sermon (khutbah) delivered by the imam on religious or community topics, followed by a shortened version of the midday prayer. For many Muslim communities, Friday prayer at the mosque is the most important gathering of the week.

3. Ramadan activities
During Ramadan (the Islamic holy month of fasting), mosques become even more active. Special night prayers called Tarawih are held after the last daily prayer, where long portions of the Quran (the holy book of Islam) are recited. Many mosques also organize iftar gatherings — communal meals to break the fast at sunset.

4. Islamic education
Mosques often serve as centers of learning. Many have attached classrooms or schools (madrasas) where children and adults learn to read the Quran, study Islamic teachings, and learn Arabic.

5. Community and social functions
A mosque is not only a spiritual space — it is also a community hub. Muslims gather there for announcements, to support one another, to celebrate religious events (like Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, the two major Islamic festivals), to solemnize marriages, and sometimes to handle community disputes. In many parts of the world, the mosque plays a role in a Muslim's life from birth to death — newborns may be brought there for blessings, and funeral prayers are conducted there before burial.

The primary users of a mosque are Muslims. However, in most parts of the world, mosques are open to non-Muslims who wish to visit respectfully. Visitors are generally expected to:

  • Remove their shoes before entering the prayer hall.
  • Dress modestly (covering arms and legs; women are usually asked to cover their hair as well).
  • Remain quiet and respectful, especially during prayer times.

Women and men typically pray in separate sections of the mosque — either in different rooms, or in the same room divided by a partition or with women in a section behind the men. The exact arrangement varies by mosque and cultural tradition.

Not all mosques look the same or serve the same role:

  • Masjid: The Arabic word for mosque. In everyday use, "mosque" and "masjid" mean the same thing — any place where Muslims perform their prayers.
  • Jama Masjid (or Grand Mosque / Friday Mosque): A larger, central mosque in a city or town that is specifically designated for Friday congregational prayers. It is typically bigger and more prominent than neighborhood mosques, and it can hold hundreds or thousands of worshippers at once.
  • Simple prayer rooms: In offices, airports, hospitals, and universities, you will sometimes find small, quiet rooms set aside for Muslims to pray. These are informally referred to as mosques or prayer rooms, even though they may just be a carpeted room with an arrow pointing toward Mecca.

Some of the world's most famous mosques include the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca (the largest mosque in the world and the holiest site in Islam, surrounding the Kaaba — the cube-shaped structure toward which all Muslims pray), the Masjid an-Nabawi in Medina (built around the tomb of the Prophet Muhammad), the Blue Mosque in Istanbul, and the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem.
How the word is used in sentences

• "There is a beautiful old mosque in the center of the city."
  • "He goes to the mosque every Friday for prayers."
  • "The mosque was built in the sixteenth century and is now a UNESCO heritage site."
  • "She visited the mosque as a tourist and was struck by the intricate tile work."
  • "After the earthquake, the local mosque served as a shelter for displaced families."

If you had to hold the whole meaning of the word in one sentence: a mosque is a building that serves as the house of worship and community center for Muslims, where they pray, learn, and come together as a religious community. It is to Islam what a church is to Christianity, a synagogue is to Judaism, or a temple is to Hinduism — the sacred, communal space at the heart of the faith.
